name: Silwerstroom
area: Atlantis coast (West Coast Road R27), north of Melkbosstrand
coord_source: Nominatim (fetched 30 Oct 2026), the 'Silwerstroomstrand Oord' resort road point at -33.58346, 18.36109. This is the resort, not a surveyed angling stand. The rocks, beach and tidal pool are on the shore just west of it. No published GPS was found for the tidal pool or the ledges.

access.note: Silwerstroomstrand Resort, on Silwerstroom Road off West Coast Road (R27). The resort and tidal pool have parking and beach access. The exact car park position is not surveyed.

bottom: Mixed. One section is rocky ledges and reef with small rock fish, and the other is sandy beach with 'even breakers' (Sealine post).
permit: A DFFE recreational angling permit is required (from the Post Office or online). The resort is a City of Cape Town facility with paid entry, per the 2026 Cape Town coastal map; the City page says the day-visitor braai areas are free entry, and the tariff sheet could not be opened. Galjoen has a closed season from 15 October to the end of February. The source found states this for the Cape Whale Coast. As far as I know it is a national rule, but no national source was checked.
legality: Fishing is allowed. Silwerstroom is on the open West Coast north of Melkbosstrand and Atlantis. It is outside the Table Mountain National Park MPA, which ends at Mouille Point, and outside the Robben Island MPA, which covers only the area around the island. No MPA restricted zone or other no-take zone applies. The City of Cape Town's Silwerstroomstrand Resort page lists fishing among the resort's activities, but gives no further rules (checked 30 Oct 2026).
description: A City of Cape Town resort beach on the open Atlantic north of Atlantis, with a rocky side and a sandy beach section next to a tidal pool. Light-tackle anglers on the rocks mostly get small rock fish (klipvis and 'blue bogger'), and tourism pages say hottentot from the shore is popular in January and February. A Western Cape fishing guide includes it in the ledge stretch from Van Riebeeckstrand to Silwerstroomstrand, which is fished for galjoen, steenbras and kob.
hazards: Open Atlantic swell breaking on low rocky ledges; risk of being washed off
Slippery, weed-covered rocks
Cold Benguela water
Remote stretch beyond Atlantis; vehicle security not documented
access_notes: The resort is on Silwerstroom Road, off West Coast Road (R27), north of Atlantis. It has paid entry (Cape Town coastal map 2026), and the City page says the day-visitor braai areas are free. Gate times are not published. The resort office is open weekdays 08:00 to 16:30 (021 444 7621, silwerstroom.resort@capetown.gov.za), and general enquiries go to 021 444 3605. The City lists low season as 1 April to 30 September. The tidal pool (3,517 m2) has picnic and braai areas and beach access. From the resort, walk onto the rocky side or the beach section.

Tide preference: no source gives one, so 'any' is a placeholder
Exact stand coordinates. The Nominatim point is the resort road; the rocks and beach are a short walk west
Galjoen, kob and steenbras catches at Silwerstroom itself. They come only from a general stretch description, with no site catch report
What species 'blue bogger' refers to
Bait and lures used here. No source names any
Typical sizes for every species

issues: 'Blue bogger' is not a fish. I fetched the Sealine thread (https://sealine.co.za/threads/koeie-by-silwerstroom.19274/, 12 Jul 2009, by 'die spook'). It says: 'het blou bogger all gevang. net lastige klipvis aan die rotsagtige kant.' 'Blou bogger all' is Afrikaans-English slang for 'bugger all', meaning nothing at all. So the line reads 'caught bugger all, only pesky klipvis on the rocky side.' The record turns this into a species, and its quote and gloss ('het blou bogger al gevang' = 'caught only blue bogger') is a mistranslation. Remove the species. Also remove 'blue bogger' from the description and from the 'unverified' list.

That angler was not fishing light tackle. He was targeting cow sharks ('koeihaaie', 'koeie', 'die lelike tannemanne'), and the thread has no replies. The description's line 'Light-tackle anglers on the rocks mostly get small rock fish' overstates it. The only site-specific angling evidence is one 2009 shark angler who mentions nuisance klipvis on the rocks and 'mooi egalige branders' on the beach section. That is enough to keep the spot (klipvis on the rocks suits light bait), but only just.

Kob and white steenbras come only from the fishingreminder Western Cape guide. Its Melkbosstrand entry runs the ledge stretch from Van Riebeeckstrand to Silwerstroomstrand and names galjoen, steenbras and kob for 'West Coast surf anglers'. The cached fetch of that page notes that no species are listed for Silwerstroom on its own. On open Atlantic ledges these are rock-and-surf targets, so method 'light bait' is not supported for kob or steenbras. 'White steenbras' is the merge step's reading of plain 'steenbras'.

Abundance and months are inferred, not sourced. Klipvis is 'common' with months [7], and the July date comes from a single 2009 post. Klipvis are a year-round inshore fish, so [7] is just the date of one outing, not a season. Klipvis 'reliably' caught on light tackle is an extrapolation. Galjoen 'occasional' and kob/steenbras 'occasional' have no basis in any source. Galjoen months [5-8] come from the guide calling Table Bay galjoen a winter fish, not from Silwerstroom.
Hottentot (Jan-Feb, 'regular') rests only on tourism pages (lekkeslaap, sa-venues), seen as a search snippet in the cache. Neither is an angling source, and the 'regular' abundance is invented.

These sources are cited but are not in the 29 Oct cache, and I did not re-check them: the City of Cape Town resort and tidal-pool pages (the claim that fishing is listed as an activity, 'checked 30 Oct'), whalecoast.info, and the OSRM drive times (51 and 64 min). The 'Paid Entry' claim from the 2026 Cape Town coastal map is backed by the search snippet. The drive times are plausible for about 60 km and 80 km on the R27, but from Westlake the spot is at or beyond the 60-minute edge.

name: Zandvlei
area: Muizenberg / Lakeside / Marina da Gama
coord_source: OSM via photon.komoot.io on 30 Oct 2026: "Imperial Yacht Club & Peninsula Canoe Club", 1 Promenade Road, Lakeside (way 672046079, point -34.0908804, 18.4668362), which matches the merge step's OSM car-park coordinate; the reserve centroid from Nominatim is -34.0919, 18.4708. The footbridge bend, sports-field bend and "bowling green" bend on the lower channel south of the yacht club are described in forum posts only and are not separately geocoded.

access.note: Imperial Yacht Club / Peninsula Canoe Club car park, 1 Promenade Road, Lakeside. The bank runs south from here along the lower channel to the footbridge and the road bridge near the mouth; the caravan park / Zandvlei Recreational Park on the east bank (Promenade Road, Muizenberg) is the other walk-in point.

bottom: Sand and silt with dense submerged pondweed beds; weed is the main snag ("you will catch them anywhere where you can cast a lure without catching weed"), and after a mouth opening the yacht-club side carries foam and silt
mouth: Managed. Open to the sea through winter; in summer the mouth is closed by a sand bar and "opened monthly for a few days at full moon to maintain salinity levels and then closed again" (Wikipedia), which Sealine posters describe as openings "at some Spring tides". Zandvlei is a City of Cape Town nature reserve, so mouth management sits with the City's reserve staff. Anglers report "no real tidal flow in that vlei" and "little to no tidal water movement", so time of day matters more than tide stage.
permit: Zandvlei is an estuary, so the DFFE permit applies, not the CapeNature licence. Bait collecting is not allowed in the reserve. Two permits cover the species mix. (1) DFFE recreational angling permit (the "Post Office permit") for the marine species: leervis, elf, mullet, springer, steenbras and stumpnose; this is the permit the Zandvlei Trust means by "obtainable from any Post Office". (2) CapeNature freshwater angling licence (valid 12 months) for the species the Western Cape Government lists under freshwater fishing for "Sandvlei: carp, Mozambique tilapia, sharptooth catfish and mullet", since "You'll need a license to fish in public rivers and dams" and licences "can be obtained from CapeNature". Local rules: leervis catch-and-release is compulsory by law (Zandvlei Trust); rod and reel only, gill nets banned (City Recreational Water Use By-law 2018). Forum posters add a City ban on live bait (2011) and closure of the reserve to anglers from sunset to sunrise under the Nature Conservation Ordinance, with officials checking permits and bag and size limits; the thread carrying this is blocked, so treat those two as unverified but plan around them (no live mullet, no night sessions).
legality: Allowed with a permit. Zandvlei is a City of Cape Town nature reserve and recreational park inland of Muizenberg beach, outside the Table Mountain National Park MPA (whose False Bay boundary is at Bailey's Cottage on the coast to the west), so no MPA no-take zone applies. Zandvlei Trust: "Zandvlei is popular with fishermen" and "A fishing permit is required which is obtainable from any Post Office or some fishing tackle shops"; Wikipedia: "Fishing is popular, with many large garrick having been landed. A standard fishing permit is required"; the City's Zandvlei Recreational Park page lists fishing among its activities; Western Cape Government lists "Sandvlei: carp, Mozambique tilapia, sharptooth catfish and mullet" under freshwater fishing waters. Local rule: "Catch and release of indigenous species such as Leervis is required by law" (Zandvlei Trust). Gill nets are banned under the City's Recreational Water Use By-law (2018), rod and reel only. Checked: Zandvlei Trust activities page, Wikipedia, both City pages, Western Cape Government fishing page (fetched 30 Oct 2026). Not checked: the reserve's Integrated Reserve Management Plan, which may define no-fishing zones; the Flytalk "Fishing Management at Zandvlei" thread that discussed the official rules is proxy-blocked.
description: Zandvlei is the shallow, weedy estuary behind Muizenberg beach, run as a City nature reserve with a managed mouth, and it is Cape Town's best-known shore water for leervis on light tackle and fly: The Mission calls it "amazing fly fishing for leervis" with "a resident population of good-sized leervis", and Sealine anglers fish the public bank "from that yacht club to the bridge near the mouth" and "the first bend after the footbridge" with small spoons, chisel-nose plugs, Zara Spooks and pink Clousers. Mullet, elf, springer, carp, catfish, tilapia, bass and juvenile steenbras and stumpnose also show; one local has taken eight species on a 9-weight "patrolling the margins". There is little tidal movement, so daybreak and dusk matter more than the tide, and every leervis must be released.
hazards: Personal safety: a reader on The Mission (18 Sep 2026) reports 'a close call' fishing 'in the early morning from the camping place' and asks whether Marina da Gama is safer; do not fish the east-bank caravan-park side alone at first light.
Dense pondweed beds foul lures and flies; fish the channels and weed edges.

Pollution: sewage and effluent incidents are reported (a 2024 reader saw a truck dumping effluent from the car park behind the water slides) and a Sealine moderator advises against eating fish from the vlei; leervis must be released anyway.
After a mouth opening the yacht-club side turns 'very discoloured, lots of foam and silt around'; the water near the footbridge cleans up first.
South-easter chop across the open vlei; the Marina da Gama channels are 'sheltered from wind'.
Marina da Gama canal frontage is largely private; use public access points.
Reserve reportedly closed to anglers from sunset to sunrise (forum claim, unverified); night carp sessions may not be lawful.
access_notes: Free entry. Park at the Imperial Yacht Club / Peninsula Canoe Club car park, 1 Promenade Road, Lakeside, and fish the public west bank from the yacht club south along the channel to the footbridge and the road bridge near the mouth (the sports-field bend and 'first bend after the footbridge' are on this stretch). The east bank is reached from the Zandvlei Recreational Park / caravan park on Promenade Road, Muizenberg (the 'camping place'); the old Sail restaurant frontage there was 'now closed off to cars' by 2009. The reserve office at Coniston Avenue, Marina da Gama, keeps Monday to Friday 07:30-16:00 and is closed weekends, but the banks are open public parkland; forum posters say the reserve is closed to fishing from sunset to sunrise (unverified). Marina da Gama canals: public access points only. Drive: about 5 minutes from Westlake and 28 minutes from Green Point (OSRM free-flow, 29 Oct 2026); no source gives a drive time.
unverified: City by-law (2011) banning live bait at Zandvlei, and closure of the reserve to anglers from sunset to sunrise under the Nature Conservation Ordinance: forum posters only, the Flytalk thread is proxy-blocked and the 4x4community thread returns 403.
Whether the reserve's Integrated Reserve Management Plan or Precinct Plan designates no-fishing zones inside the reserve: not read.
Depth and bottom composition: no source gives figures; 'shallow' and 'sand and silt' are inferred from the shallow-banks, weed-bed and silt descriptions.
Elf season (Dec-Mar) is taken from the adjacent Muizenberg surf thread, not a vlei-specific report; no source gives seasons for springer, carp, catfish, tilapia, bass, stumpnose or steenbras.
Baits for tilapia, bass, stumpnose and steenbras in the vlei: not stated by any source.
That most of the Marina da Gama canal frontage is private: merge-step note, no page quoted.

Cape moonie ('some moonies') is a single historical recollection from the 1950s on and is left off the species list; spotted grunter has only ever been trek-netted at the mouth, never taken on rod and reel, and kob is not reported in the vlei.
The 'bowling green' bend and 'Uitsig Point' positions are not geocoded.

issues: Legality holds. Zandvlei is a City estuary reserve behind Muizenberg beach, east of Bailey's Cottage, so it sits outside the TMNP MPA and outside the Helderberg and Robben Island MPAs. The Zandvlei Trust activities page says 'Zandvlei is popular with fishermen' and 'A fishing permit is required which is obtainable from any Post Office'. Wikipedia says 'A standard fishing permit is required'. No source in the cache names a no-fishing zone.

Permit claim verified by a new fetch of westerncape.gov.za/fishing-western-cape (2 Nov 2026). Under 'Freshwater fishing' it lists 'Sandvlei: carp, Mozambique tilapia, sharptooth catfish and mullet', and it says 'You'll need a license to fish in public rivers and dams. Licenses can be obtained from CapeNature ... valid for 12 months'. The page names DAFF offices, not the Post Office, as the source of saltwater permits; the Post Office wording comes from the Zandvlei Trust. The record lists mullet under both permits, which is harmless but not clean.

The rule 'Catch and release of indigenous species such as Leervis is required by law' rests only on the Zandvlei Trust page. A search summary in the cache gives the general national leervis rules as a 70 cm minimum size and a bag of 2. The record should say this is the Trust's statement of a reserve rule, not quoted regulation text.

Unresolved hours issue that matters for an hour-by-hour rating: both City nature-reserve pages give 'Monday to Friday 07:30 to 16:00' and 'Closed on weekends'. The record reads these as office hours only and says the banks are open public parkland, but no source says so. Add this to the forum claim (Flytalk, proxy-blocked) that the vlei is closed to anglers from sunset to sunrise under the 1974 Ordinance, and the record's advice to fish 'first light (even before)' and at night for carp may not be lawful. Flag it rather than state it as fact.
Neither City nature-reserve page (Explore and enjoy, Family and home) mentions fishing. Only the Recreational Park page lists it, and the cache has that page only as a search summary.

Evidence is strong and fits light tackle. Sealine 18196 has bank spinning 'from that yacht club to the bridge near the mouth' and 'the first bend after the footbridge' with spoons, chisel-nose plugs and Zara Spooks. Sealine 3974 has a chisel-nose plug, spinners and fly. Sean Mills (2013 blog) says 'the best areas are close to the mouth in the area of the foot bridge'. The Mission's Andy Killick piece (fetched 2 Nov 2026) describes a 9-weight floating-line setup, 'patrolling the margins' and 'a short fishing session around daybreak in Zandvlei'.

species.size: Mostly small; 'some big harders' and 'big mullet' near the weed beds
species.bait: #14 hare's ear nymph for average mullet; large white streamers near weed beds for big mullet (Sean Mills)
species.notes: Listed by the Western Cape Government as a freshwater species for Sandvlei (CapeNature licence). One poster netted mullet at Surfers Corner for catfish bait; mullet is also the live bait old posts used for leervis. No season given.

species.size: Not stated
species.bait: Mullet (netted at Surfers Corner) fished as bait
species.notes: CapeNature freshwater licence applies. A Sealine moderator advises against eating fish from the vlei because of pollution.

species.size: Typically to about 6 kg ('never seen one over 6kg'); one 10 kg fish taken at night
species.bait: TCP mielies with a TCP/banana dip, cake-flour dough coloured red (curry powder added by one poster), bread crust for sighted fish; also taken on fly
species.notes: CapeNature freshwater licence applies (Western Cape Government lists carp for Sandvlei). The 10 kg fish came at night, which conflicts with the reported sunset-to-sunrise closure.

species.size: Mostly 50-80 cm (roughly 2-5 kg) fish; the vlei holds 'good-sized' resident fish, with a 12 kg fish on a spinner and a 24 kg fish on fly (2004) reported, and Sean Mills calls them 'among the largest in the area'
species.bait: Surface plugs (Zara Spook, Super Spook, Skitter Pop, Chug Bug), light-pink chisel-nose plugs, small Abu Toby / Koster / Hopkins Shorty spoons in copper or chrome, bucktail leadheads, Rebel minnows; fly on a 9-weight with a floating line: pink Clouser, Deceiver, brush flies, poppers and Richard Wale's 'Stella' topwater; live mullet under a float is mentioned in old posts but would fall under the reported live-bait ban
species.notes: Catch and release required by law; 'a very limited population of fish in there' that 'can get hammered by the catch and fillet boys'. Low light: 'You need to be there first light (even before)', 'sunrise and sunset are garrick catching times', one angler had most strikes late afternoon; Andy Killick gets 'a better hook-up rate fishing in low-light with a fast retrieve' and 'many follows that end in refusals'. Subsurface Clousers and Deceivers stripped in after sinking drew more strikes than poppers for one angler; surface flies in early summer. Stands: near the mouth around the footbridge at sunrise (Sean Mills: 'the best areas are close to the mouth in the area of the foot bridge'), the channel running from the yacht club, 'the first bend after the footbridge', the bend at the sports fields, the bowling green bend, Uitsig Point and 1st channel, the main island, and up into Marina da Gama ('guys catch them all the way up to Marina Da Gama'). Season from posts: six fish in December, 'really warm days in summer', February; June described as less active.

species.notes: CapeNature freshwater licence applies (listed for Sandvlei by the Western Cape Government).

species.size: Not stated; small estuary fish are the norm

name: Little Princess Vlei
area: Bergvliet / Heathfield, southern suburbs, between the M3 and M5
coord_source: photon.komoot.io (OSM natural=water "Little Princess Vlei", Cape Town Ward 72): -34.0474403, 18.4746145, matching Fishbrain's 34°02′51.4″S 18°28′28.2″E. This is the water-body centroid, not a verified bank stand; no source gives a car park or entry point. Nominatim was blocked when the cache was built.
bottom: Not described by any source; likely sand and silt with weed beds, as is typical of Cape Flats vleis (unverified).
permit: A CapeNature recreational freshwater angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance) is required for any public inland water in the Western Cape, but it does not override the City's moratorium: the City's Recreation and Parks Department instituted a moratorium on angling at City dams in 2005 and, per its 18 Feb 2020 release, only Doordekraal Dam (Oct-Apr, with permits) is exempt. No City permit scheme for this vlei was found.
legality: Not established, and probably prohibited. Fresh water, so no MPA zoning applies. Checked: the City of Cape Town media release of 18 Feb 2020, "To fish or not to fish, that is the question" ("In 2005, a moratorium was instituted on angling at City dams", citing anti-social behaviour and injuries to aquatic birds; Doordekraal Dam in Durbanville the only exception, with limited controlled fishing Oct-Apr with permits under a 2007 compromise; a feasibility study of "more than 60 open water bodies" done and a public participation process pending); the City's Princess Vlei Conservation Area page (the larger vlei; lists nature appreciation, environmental education and walking only, no fishing); the City's freshwater-fishing page (CapeNature licence needed for public waters, no waters named); CapeNature's recreational fishing permit page; and a targeted web search on 30 Oct 2026, which found no page stating that angling is allowed or prohibited at Little Princess Vlei specifically. Neither Sealine nor Fishbrain addresses legality. Little Princess Vlei is a City-managed open water body in a public open space, not a nature reserve with its own angling permit scheme like Zandvlei or Rietvlei, so the City moratorium is the best available statement of its status.
description: Little Princess Vlei (Klein Prinsesvlei) is a small City-owned vlei in Bergvliet/Heathfield between the M3 and M5, about ten minutes from Westlake, and is distinct from the larger Princess Vlei conservation area off Prince George Drive that it drains into. Fishbrain logs 47 catches here and calls it "most popular for fishing Largemouth bass, F1 carp, and Common carp", and a 2019 Sealine thread describes bank fishing for "very very smart and some quite big bass that have every lure thrown at them all day long", while warning of "not so much bank access and lots of rubbish" and poor personal safety. The City instituted a moratorium on angling at its dams in 2005 and, as of its February 2020 statement, only Doordekraal Dam was exempt; nothing found says this vlei has been opened, so it is dropped.
hazards: Personal safety: the Sealine moderator says the area is 'not so much anymore, never used to be so safe' and fishes it with an armed, military-trained friend and dogs (22 Jul 2019).
'Lots of rubbish' on the banks (Sealine).
'Not so much bank access': few open casting spots on an urban vlei with reedy, built-up edges (Sealine).
access_notes: Public City open space in Bergvliet/Heathfield between the M3 and M5, about 10 min from Westlake and 26 min from Green Point (OSRM free-flow estimate). The only angling source says there is 'not so much bank access and lots of rubbish'; no source gives parking, an entry point, hours or fees. Children fish the feeder canal for small bass. Angling falls under the City's 2005 moratorium on fishing at City dams unless the City has since opened this vlei; a CapeNature freshwater angling licence would be required in any case.
unverified: Whether the City's post-2020 review of its open water bodies has opened Little Princess Vlei to angling: no source found either way, so the 2005 moratorium is assumed to still apply.
Kurper (banded tilapia): Sealine says only 'Most likely kurper as they are in the system'; a presumption, no catch reported.
Sharptooth catfish (barbel): the merge took this from Fishbrain's separate Princess Vlei page (the larger vlei off the M5), not from the Little Princess Vlei page, which lists no catfish.
'F1 carp' on Fishbrain (2 members) is treated as common carp logged under Fishbrain's F1 label.
Depth and bottom: no source describes them; 'shallow' and sand/silt with weed are inferred from the vlei's character.
Parking, entry point, hours and fees: no source; the coordinate given is the water-body centroid, not a bank stand.

A search-summary mention of 'a small bass caught off a float tube at Princess Vlei in Muizenberg' (The Mission fly mag) could not be traced on the magazine's site, was from a float tube rather than the shore, and probably refers to the larger vlei.
Which canal the Sealine poster means by 'the feeder canal' is not identified.
legal_note: no City of Cape Town page says angling is allowed or banned here. The conservation area's page lists walking, nature appreciation and education only, and the City's 2020 statement on its angling moratorium covers City dams without naming the vleis. Check with the City's Princess Vlei Conservation Area before you fish.

species.size: 'Some quite big bass' per Sealine, with small bass in the feeder canal that children fish for; no measured sizes in any source.
species.bait: Lures. The Sealine account describes working a skirted jig with a trailer at a nesting fish that 'took the bait lightly, by the trailer or skirt', and says the bass 'have every lure thrown at them all day long', so they are pressured and lure-shy. Fishbrain names no lures.

name: Liesbeek River (Observatory)
aka: Liesbeek River, lower reaches (Observatory to Mowbray)
area: Observatory / Mowbray, Cape Town (Hartleyvale, Liesbeek Parkway)
coord_source: Nominatim (OpenStreetMap) result for "Hartleyvale Stadium", fetched 30 Oct 2026: -33.9390112, 18.4758075. This is the same point the merge step used as its rough coordinate (the OSM stadium node, not a point on the water); the river runs along the east side of Hartleyvale beside Liesbeek Parkway. bottom: Slow, reed-fringed natural channel in the lower reach past Hartleyvale (the City page describes birds hiding "in the reeds across the river"); soft silt or mud bottom is inferred, not sourced. Upstream the middle reaches (Rondebosch to Mowbray) are concrete canal ("much of the middle reaches of the river are canalised", Friends of the Liesbeek).
permit: CapeNature freshwater angling licence, required for anyone over six fishing public rivers and dams; R45 (CapeNature page), valid 12 months from issue (Western Cape Government page). Apply by emailing the form, supporting documents and proof of payment to permits.fax@capenature.co.za (2 to 5 working days), or through CapeNature head office 087 087 9262 or a regional office. Release indigenous species; no bag limits stated for carp or sharptooth catfish. No City permit or entry fee is published for the Liesbeek Parkway bank or the Raapenberg Bird Sanctuary.
legality: Fishing is allowed with a licence. The Liesbeek is a public river named on CapeNature's recreational fishing permit page (opened 29 Oct 2026) among the rivers the licence covers ("Rivers: Berg, Breede ..., Eerste, Lourens, and Liesbeek"), under section 53 of the Nature Conservation Ordinance ("no person may fish in any inland waters without an angling licence"). The Western Cape Government fishing page (opened 29 Oct 2026) lists it under "The different locations where the public can go fishing", with "The lower reaches have large numbers of carp and sharptooth catfish". The Hartleyvale-to-SAAO stretch is the City of Cape Town's Raapenberg Bird Sanctuary (a "biodiversity park"); its page (fetched 30 Oct 2026) lists "River access" as a feature and "Nature appreciation", "Picnics and braaing", "Sport and exercise" as activities, and does not mention fishing either way. A web search for a bylaw or "no fishing" rule on the Liesbeek, Raapenberg, Two Rivers Urban Park or Liesbeek Parkway found none. Indigenous fish (Cape kurper, Cape galaxias) must be returned to the water; the CapeNature page states no bag or size limits for carp or catfish. The Fishing Owl "Liesbeek Ghosts" journal page returned 404, so no page was blocked.
description: The lower Liesbeek is a small urban river running beside Liesbeek Parkway from Mowbray to its confluence with the Black River at Observatory; CapeNature and the Western Cape Government both list it as a public fishing water whose "lower reaches have large numbers of carp and sharptooth catfish", and the Jacita fishing report (June 2025) says "Find large carp and catfish in the lower stretches". Friends of the Liesbeek place carp, catfish, the odd trout and shrimps "lower down, in the slower flowing parts of the river", with the middle reaches (Rondebosch to Mowbray) running in concrete canal. It is bank fishing from a public park with a CapeNature freshwater licence; no source describes the tackle used, so light bait on small hooks or a fly rod is an inference from the species and the size of the water.
hazards: Polluted urban river: the City's Raapenberg page lists 'rehabilitate the polluted rivers' as a management priority; avoid contact with the water and wash hands before eating.
Busy Liesbeek Parkway runs directly along the bank (the City page calls it 'the busy Liesbeek Parkway').
Soft, reedy banks on the lower reach; vertical concrete canal walls with no easy exit on the canalised stretch upstream (Mowbray to Rondebosch).
Small catchment: winter storm flows rise quickly; summer flow reportedly drops to a trickle (search snippet only, unverified).
Urban park: fish in daylight and keep valuables out of sight in the car (general advice, not a sourced incident).
access_notes: Park at Hartleyvale Stadium / Observatory Road or along Liesbeek Parkway; the City lists picnic sites 'along the busy Liesbeek Parkway' and 'River access' as a feature of the Raapenberg Bird Sanctuary (the stretch 'between the Hartleyvale football ground and the South African Astronomical Observatory'). A walking path follows the river through Observatory. No opening hours, gates or fees are published for the Parkway bank; City general enquiries 021 701 1233. Drive: about 12 minutes from Green Point and 21 minutes from Westlake (OSRM free-flow, 2026-10-29).
unverified: No page describes the tackle or method used on the Liesbeek; 'light bait on small hooks or a fly rod from the bank' is inferred from the species and the size of the river, not quoted from an angler.

No first-hand angler account (forum, club or journal) of fishing the lower Liesbeek was found; the only angling-specific source is the Jacita weekly fishing report, which lists the river without methods.
Exact stand: no source names one; the coordinate is the OSM Hartleyvale Stadium node, with the river along its east side.

City of Cape Town rules for the Raapenberg Bird Sanctuary stretch (Hartleyvale to the SAAO): the City page lists 'River access' and no fishing prohibition, but gives no explicit permission either; check signage or call 021 701 1233.

Trout: named as present by Friends of the Liesbeek and Wikipedia, but no catch report found; the Fishing Owl 'Liesbeek Ghosts' journal (http://www.fishingowl.co.za/fishingjournal1.html) returned 404 on 30 Oct 2026.
Mozambique tilapia: the Wikipedia page (via a search snippet) lists it among introduced species; no angling source mentions it here, so it is left off the species list.
Summer flow 'reduced to a trickle' by abstraction: a search snippet carried over from the merge step, not confirmed.
Best months, typical sizes and baits: no Liesbeek-specific source; Jacita only says 'large carp', and the months given are the general warm-water season for carp and catfish.
Soft silt or mud bottom in the lower reach is inferred from the slow, reed-fringed character the sources describe, not stated by any page.

issues: Legality holds. This is inland fresh water, nowhere near an MPA. CapeNature's recreational fishing permit page (cached 29 Oct 2026) names the Liesbeek among the licensed rivers, with 'The lower reaches have large numbers of carp and sharptooth catfish'. The Western Cape Government page lists it under 'The different locations where the public can go fishing'. R45, 12-month validity and head office 087 087 9262 all match the cache.

The record's own Raapenberg Bird Sanctuary (City of Cape Town) evidence is not in the cache. That City page and the Friends of the Liesbeek ecology page were fetched on 30 Oct, so I could not check them against the cache, including the 'River access' feature, the absence of a fishing rule and the 'polluted rivers' quote. Whether fishing is allowed on City land beside the bank is still an open question, not a confirmed permission.

The 'three independent sources' claim in the reason is overstated. Jacita's June 2025 freshwater section is a rewrite of the Western Cape Government list, in the same order (Voelvlei, Lakensvlei, Brandvlei, Rietvlei, Misverstand, Sandvlei, Theewaterskloof, Zeekoevlei, Berg, Breede, Eerste/Lourens, Liesbeek), with the same one line for the Liesbeek. The Western Cape Government and CapeNature pages share their wording too, and the Western Cape Government page still says DAFF, so the text is old. All the evidence comes down to one official sentence of unknown age. No angler-written page, forum thread, club page or catch report describes fishing the lower Liesbeek.

Evidence is not refuted, because CapeNature's permit page is angling-specific and names the river as public fishing water for carp and catfish, which suits light bait fishing from the bank. But it is thin: no source gives a method, a stand or a catch.

The coordinates hold, but the point is not on the water. Overpass (OSM) puts the natural 'Liesbeeck River' channel (way 4349758) at about lon 18.4776 at lat -33.9390, roughly 160 m east of the Hartleyvale Stadium node (18.4758). The natural reach beside Hartleyvale runs only from about -33.9436 (where the canal from Mowbray ends) to a weir at -33.9364. Below the weir it splits into the 'Liesbeeck Canal' and a western river branch, so the 'Observatory to Mowbray' natural stretch is really about 800 m beside Hartleyvale.

The Hartleyvale coordinate (coord_source 'Nominatim ... fetched 30 Oct') cannot be checked against the cache. Every cached Nominatim query for Hartleyvale returned HTTP 429. The Overpass geometry is consistent with it, though.

name: Door De Kraal Dam
area: Bellville (Door de Kraal / Welgemoed), on the Durbanville border
coord_source: photon.komoot.io geocode fetched 2026-10-30: OSM water feature "Door De Kraal Dam", city Bellville, at lon 18.629331 lat -33.8642152, which matches the merge-step coordinates. This is the OSM point for the dam itself, not a surveyed bank stand or car park; no source describes where anglers stand or park.
bottom: Not stated in any source.
permit: The City of Cape Town's only open angling dam: a City permit as well as the CapeNature licence, in season from October to April. CapeNature recreational freshwater angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance; anyone over six fishing public waters) applied for via capenature.co.za, as required by the City's freshwater-fishing page and quoted in the 2025 Weekend Argus report. The City also refers to "the relevant permits" for this dam, which reads as a City-side permit on top of the CapeNature licence; how and where that is issued was not found online, so confirm with the City's Recreation and Parks Department before fishing. Season: October to April only.
legality: Allowed with permits, in season only. City of Cape Town media release "To fish or not to fish, that is the question" (18 Feb 2020, opened 29 Oct 2026): a 2005 moratorium banned angling at City dams after complaints about antisocial behaviour and injuries to waterbirds, but since 2007 Doordekraal Dam has had "limited and controlled fishing" "between October and April and with the relevant permits", the only City dam named as open; other dams were under a feasibility review. Weekend Argus, 29 Jul 2025 (opened 29 Oct 2026): the City urges anglers to "obtain a permit and fish exclusively at designated City sites, such as Door De Kraal Dam in Bellville", says "all anglers must obtain a CapeNature recreational fishing licence" and that fishing without a valid permit is illegal; nearby Rosendal Dam has no-fishing signage and people were fined at Vierlanden Dam. Inland, so no MPA zoning applies. The City's own freshwater-fishing page (fetched 2026-10-30) names no dams and only restates the CapeNature licence rule for public waters.
description: Door De Kraal Dam is a small suburban park dam in Bellville, on the Durbanville border, and the only City of Cape Town dam where angling is allowed: the City's 18 February 2020 release says that while a 2005 moratorium closed angling at City dams, Doordekraal Dam has since 2007 had "limited and controlled fishing" "between October and April and with the relevant permits", and in July 2025 the City was still telling Durbanville anglers to "obtain a permit and fish exclusively at designated City sites, such as Door De Kraal Dam in Bellville". Sealine anglers name it for bass and carp ("Doordekraal can be fished with permit and floattube", June 2020) and one recalls a second-hand 21 kg carp from the late 1990s. Light bait for carp or a light spinning rod for bass fits the water, but no page describes a bank stand and the one dated session (July 2020) produced no bites, so treat it as a quiet, permit-and-season venue rather than a sure thing.
hazards: No physical hazards reported in any source.

Waterbirds: injuries to aquatic birds from discarded line are the City's stated reason for the dam moratorium, and the 2025 report describes a goose trapped in line at a neighbouring dam; take every scrap of line home.
Enforcement: City Law Enforcement patrols Durbanville-area dams and fines illegal anglers; fishing here out of season or without the CapeNature licence and City permit risks a fine.
access_notes: Suburban City park dam in Bellville's Door de Kraal/Welgemoed area; no source gives parking, a walk, hours or a usual stand. Fishing is allowed only October to April with "the relevant permits" (City of Cape Town, 18 Feb 2020). Carry a CapeNature freshwater licence; the City-side permit arrangement was not found online, so check with Recreation and Parks before going. Nearby Rosendal, Sonstraal and Vierlanden dams are not legal sites.
unverified: That anglers fish it from the bank: the only angling-page mention says "with permit and floattube"; bank fishing is inferred from it being a suburban park dam and from the City's "limited and controlled fishing" wording.
How the City-side permit is issued (office, cost, day or season permit); only the CapeNature licence is documented.
Whether the October to April window from the 2020 release is still the rule in 2026; the 2025 Weekend Argus quote confirms the site but gives no season.
Depth and bottom: no source; shallow is an assumption for a small suburban stormwater dam.
Catch rates and sizes: the only dated session (July 2020) had no bites and the 21 kg carp is a second-hand 1990s recollection.
Parking, hours and the usual stand.

issues: Legality holds up. In its 18 Feb 2020 release (cached 29 Oct 2026) the City of Cape Town says the 2005 moratorium closed angling at City dams, but that since 2007 Doordekraal Dam has had limited, controlled fishing from October to April with the relevant permits. The Weekend Argus piece of 29 Jul 2025 (cached) tells anglers to fish 'exclusively at designated City sites, such as Door De Kraal Dam in Bellville'. The dam is inland, so no MPA applies, and it is not a water-supply dam.

The description overstates the City position. It calls this 'the only City of Cape Town dam where angling is allowed' in the present tense. That is true of the 2020 release only. The 2025 Argus wording is 'designated City sites, such as Door De Kraal Dam', which suggests there may now be other designated sites. The wording should be dated to 2020, or describe the dam as 'the designated site the City names'.

Season is unconfirmed for 2026. The October to April window appears only in the 2020 release. The cached extract of the 2025 Argus says 'No fishing season or seasonal restrictions are mentioned.' The record already flags this, but the 'Season: October to April only' line in the permit field reads as settled fact.

No source describes bank fishing. The only description of how the water is fished is the Sealine bass thread (Aubrey Mynhardt, 9 Jun 2020): 'Doordekraal can be fished with permit and floattube'. A float tube is not shore fishing. Nitesh's no-bite session on 27 Jul 2020 does not say where he fished from. The cached evidence therefore supports angling for light-tackle species, but bank fishing is an inference. I did not set evidence_refuted because the sources are angling and official pages, not tourism pages, and the target species fit light tackle.

The bass attribution is thin. In the cached extract of the bass thread, 'bass and carp' at Doordekraal partly comes from what Nitesh fished for (he fished Hillcrest for bass and carp the same way), so it does not clearly confirm that bass live in the dam. 'Largemouth' is assumed, and the record says so.

Carp is confirmed independently. I re-fetched the carp thread on 2 Nov 2026. Stefan Engelbrecht (post #13, 9 Sep 2011) wrote: 'I spoke to a friend of a friend who caught a 21kg carp in Doordekraal in the late 1990's if I remember correctly.' gt40 (post #10, 9 Sep 2011) wrote that 'some dams around bellville/durbanville' hold fish of 12-17 kg, without naming one. The record quotes both accurately. The thread was not in the 29 Oct cache, but it checks out.

species.size: No typical size given. The only figures are a second-hand "21kg carp in Doordekraal in the late 1990's" and a poster's claim that unnamed Bellville/Durbanville dams hold fish of 12-17 kg, so expect ordinary park-dam carp with the odd big one.
species.bait: Not stated for this dam. The usual Cape park-dam carp baits (sweetcorn, bread, floaties or small boilies on a light ledger or float rig, small hooks) are the sensible default, but no source names a bait here.
species.notes: Named with bass by Aubrey Mynhardt on Sealine (9 Jun 2020); Nitesh fished it for bass and carp on 27 Jul 2020 and had no bites. The 21 kg fish is Stefan Engelbrecht's second-hand recollection (Sealine, 9 Sep 2011) with no method given. Fishing is only allowed October to April, which also covers the warm months carp feed best.

species.size: Not stated in any source.
species.bait: Not stated for this dam. Standard light-tackle bass lures (small paddle-tails, dropshot, small spinnerbaits or crankbaits) are the general choice, not a spot-specific tip.
species.notes: Offered as an option in a Sealine bass thread: "Doordekraal can be fished with permit and floattube" (Aubrey Mynhardt, 9 Jun 2020), with bass and carp named. The one dated session (Nitesh, 27 Jul 2020, mid-winter) produced no bites. Species is given as bass; largemouth is assumed, as for other Cape dams.

name: Rietvlei
aka: Table Bay Nature Reserve, Rietvlei section
Rietvlei dam (local usage; not the Rietvlei Dam near Pretoria)
area: Table View / Milnerton (Flamingo Vlei)
coord_source: Nominatim (OSM) query 2026-10-30 for "Milnerton Aquatic Club, Sandpiper Crescent, Flamingo Vlei": -33.8368186, 18.4940143 (leisure/sports_centre). The Friends of Rietvlei directions page says you park at the end of Grey Avenue and "enter the reserve through the gate to the Milnerton Aquatic Club", and the Sealine thread says you "go in through the gates where all the boats launch from and they will tell you where to fish", so the gate is used as the stand; the designated bank fishing sites along the vlei are not mapped by any source. The reserve centroid from the 29 October 2026 Nominatim query (Rietvlei Wetland Reserve) is -33.8457, 18.4999.

access.note: Parking area on the right at the end of Grey Avenue, Table View; walk in through the Milnerton Aquatic Club gate, pay the entry and fishing tariff, sign the code of conduct, and the ranger assigns you one of the open fishing sites near the boat-launch area.

bottom: Soft silt and sand with reed and bulrush margins; the pan is the deep-water section of the wetland used by the Milnerton Aquatic Club for sailing, power boating and windsurfing. Bottom and depth are not stated by any source.
mouth: Not an estuary at the fishing sites: the open-water pan sits above the Diep River / Milnerton Lagoon estuary, whose mouth forum posters said has been open for years; the vlei is treated as fresh water (CapeNature freshwater licence).
permit: Table Bay Nature Reserve: fishing at the designated sites only, within reserve hours, with a reserve fishing fee; rod and reel only, two rods with two hooks each, line no stronger than 4.5 kg; carp and barbel must not be returned. CapeNature recreational freshwater angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance s53; valid 12 months from issue; CapeNature's page quotes R45, possibly outdated) PLUS City of Cape Town reserve entry (per person and per vehicle) and a per-visit fishing tariff paid at the gate (amount in the City's nature conservation tariffs; Sealine posters recalled roughly R30-35 per person or per rod in 2008-2010). Local rules per Friends of Rietvlei: designated sites only; rod and reel only; two rods per person, max two hooks per rod; line max 4.5 kg breaking strain (a Milnerton Aquatic Club rule to protect skiers and windsurfers); all discarded line removed; carp and barbel must be removed from the water, indigenous species returned; fill out specimen labels for fish caught; sign the Blaauwberg Administration code of conduct; tour operators must book and may not use more than 60% of the sites. No DFFE marine permit needed for the vlei.
legality: Allowed with conditions. The vlei is an inland City of Cape Town nature reserve (Table Bay Nature Reserve, Rietvlei section), outside every MPA in the brief (the Table Mountain NP MPA ends at Mouille Point; Robben Island MPA is around the island only), so DFFE marine zoning does not apply. Friends of Rietvlei's fishing page: "Fishing is allowed but various regulations apply"; anglers need a CapeNature freshwater permit ("In terms of section 53 of the Ordinance no person may fish in any inland waters without an angling licence"), must sign an agreement to follow the Blaauwberg Administration guidelines, fish only at the designated sites "between the reserve's official opening and closing times (07:30 to 17:00 daily)", and are "subject to inspections at the access gate or at the fishing site". The Sealine thread confirms "there is only one section that is open for fishing" with a per-person fee each visit. After the 2024 flood closures the City's reopening notice (IOL, 20 Aug 2024, via search) listed "fishing at selected sites" with a freshwater permit required. The current City reserve page could not be opened (timed out twice on 2026-10-30); its search snippet gives hours 07:30-16:00 with exit by 17:00 and says fishing permit charges are in the City's nature conservation tariffs for 1 July 2026-30 June 2027. Confirm site availability with the ranger or tablebay.naturereserve@capetown.gov.za / 021 444 0315.
description: Rietvlei is the permanent open-water pan of the Diep River wetland inside the City of Cape Town's Table Bay Nature Reserve at Flamingo Vlei, Table View, entered through the Milnerton Aquatic Club gate at the end of Grey Avenue. Bank fishing is allowed only at the designated "fishing sites along the vlei" that the ranger points you to, in reserve hours, "only the rod and reel method", "two rods per person with a maximum of two hooks per rod" and line with a "maximum breaking strength of 4,5 kg", with a CapeNature freshwater licence and a gate fee. Carp are the main target (they "bite like no tomorrow at times" per the Sealine carp forum, though mostly small), with kurper (Mozambique tilapia) and harders caught at the same spots; carp and barbel must be removed, indigenous fish returned.
hazards: Fish die-offs from low oxygen reported by Sealine posters; water quality in the Diep River / Rietvlei / Milnerton Lagoon system is chronically poor with sewage spills from the Potsdam works upstream (2026 pollution report), so avoid contact with the water after spills and do not eat the fish
Water-skiers, sailors and windsurfers share the pan (Milnerton Aquatic Club), which is why the 4.5 kg line limit exists
Reserve closes after flooding (closed in the 2024 winter floods, reopened August 2024 with fishing at selected sites only) and on a few closed days a year
Soft, reedy, muddy banks
access_notes: Park in the area on the right at the end of Grey Avenue, Table View, and enter through the Milnerton Aquatic Club gate; pay entry (per person and per vehicle) plus the fishing tariff at the gate, sign the Blaauwberg Administration code of conduct, and the ranger assigns the fishing site (only one section is open, with pre-marked borders; one poster believed about six groups at a time). Hours: Friends of Rietvlei says 07:30 to 17:00 daily; the City page (search snippet) says 07:30 to 16:00 with exit by 17:00; fishing only in opening hours. Anglers are subject to inspection at the gate and at the site. Two Sealine posters thought the combined car, entry and fishing fees made it "not worth the effort". Contact: 021 444 0315, tablebay.naturereserve@capetown.gov.za.

Depth and bottom of the pan: no source states them
Baits, lures and best months for every species: no source gives them for this spot; general patterns are stated and labelled as such
Sharptooth catfish: presence inferred from the reserve's remove-exotics rule, no catch report
Leervis and white steenbras: a single pre-2008 recollection on Sealine, no recent report
