issues: Legality holds. Rietvlei is an inland City of Cape Town reserve and sits outside every MPA in the brief. Friends of Rietvlei's fishing page (cached 29 Oct 2026) says 'Fishing is allowed but various regulations apply' and requires a CapeNature freshwater licence (Ordinance s53). The 2024 reopening notice (search snippet) lists 'fishing at selected sites'. The 2026 City page snippet still points to fishing-permit tariffs, so fishing has not been dropped. The only official City page in the evidence is a search snippet, though: the page itself was never opened. Current status therefore rests on a 2006-2014 friends page plus snippets, and medium confidence is the right level.

The reason field calls the Friends of Rietvlei 'Fishing in Rietvlei' page 'an angling club page'. It is not: it is a conservation friends-group page that copies the City/Blaauwberg rules. The only angling-specific source is the Sealine Carp Angling thread (2008-2010). Evidence is still not refuted, because that thread describes bank fishing at marked sections with carp, kurper and harders, and the 4.5 kg line limit suits light tackle.

Coordinates confirmed. A new Nominatim search on 2026-11-02 for 'Milnerton Aquatic Club' returns -33.8368186, 18.4940143 (leisure/sports_centre, Sandpiper Crescent, Flamingo Vlei), which matches the record. Friends of Rietvlei's directions page confirms you enter the reserve 'through the gate to the Milnerton Aquatic Club'. The point is the entry gate, not a mapped fishing site; the record already says so.

The route wording does not match the directions page. The record says turn 'right onto Grey Avenue at the four-way stop and carry on to the end'. The fetched directions page (2026-11-02) says to carry on along Pentz Drive to the four-way stop where it crosses Grey Avenue, continue to the end of Pentz Drive, and turn right there, with 'a parking area on the right'. The access note, coord_source and drive_hint all say 'end of Grey Avenue', which this source does not support.

Sharptooth catfish (barbel) is not supported as a species present here. Its only mention is the generic rule 'All exotic fish (carp and barbel) would have to be removed'. The Sealine thread does not mention barbel. Wikipedia's reserve fish list (SA Biodiversity database, 2010) names only two aliens: carp and mosquitofish. That list contradicts barbel presence. The 'occasional' abundance is invented.

White steenbras: the only source is one Sealine poster recalling 'steenies' from the past. In Cape slang 'steenie' can mean steentjie as well as steenbras, so the species mapping is uncertain. The record dates the recollection 'from before 2008', but the thread ran 2008-2010 and no date for the recollected period is given.

species.size: Mostly small; a 5-6 kg fish is caught "once in a blue moon" (KeithP), though another poster said 6-8 kg fish are "a regular down there"; bigger carp recalled from earlier years.
species.bait: Sources do not name baits; ledgered or float-fished bait on light line (4.5 kg breaking strain is the maximum allowed). Standard Cape vlei carp baits (mielies, floaties, dough) are the norm but are not sourced for this spot.
species.notes: Sealine carp forum (2008-2010): carp "bite like no tomorrow at times" but large fish are rare; the venue has hosted an annual carp competition. Provincial list: "Rietvlei: carp and Mozambique tilapia". Exotic: reserve rule says carp must be removed, not returned. Months are the general warm-season carp pattern, not sourced for this spot.

species.size: Not stated; 20-30 cm is the usual run of harders (unsourced).
species.bait: Not specified by sources; tiny hooks with bread or dough under a float, or small bread flies. Throw-netting is not an option here: rod and reel only.
species.notes: Wikipedia on the reserve: "the most abundant fish in the wetland being Liza richardsonii" (southern mullet). Sealine poster caught harders at the carp spots, and an older poster recalled "mullet, steenies and the occasional leerie". Indigenous, so must be returned.

species.size: Not stated by sources; hand-size to about 1 kg is typical at Cape vleis (unsourced).
species.bait: Not specified by sources; small hooks with earthworm or bread under a float is the usual approach. Small flies or micro soft plastics in summer are a general tilapia method, not sourced here.
species.notes: Sealine poster Dorado75 caught kurper at the same spots as the carp; the Western Cape government / CapeNature list names "Rietvlei: carp and Mozambique tilapia". Not one of the two exotics the reserve says to remove, so return it unless the ranger says otherwise. Summer months are the general tilapia pattern, not sourced for this spot.

species.size: Not stated.
species.bait: Historic only; no method given. Paddle-tails, spoons and mullet-pattern flies are the general leervis approach, not sourced here.
species.notes: Historic: a Sealine poster (Trophy) recalled "mullet, steenies and the occasional leerie" from earlier years. No report since; the vlei fishery is treated as freshwater. Protected indigenous species, catch and release.

species.size: Not stated.
species.bait: Historic only; no bait given.
species.notes: Historic: the same Sealine recollection ("steenies") from before 2008. No recent report. Indigenous, must be returned.

name: Berg River at Paarl
aka: Berg River at Paarl (Arboretum and footbridge reach)
area: Paarl, Drakenstein (Cape Winelands): the town reach of the Berg River beside the Arboretum
coord_source: Nominatim, query "Paarl Arboretum" (cached 29 Oct 2026): the centroid of the Arboretum park (-33.7516972, 18.9736304), which runs along the Berg River in Paarl. This is approximate and only an anchor. No angling source names a specific stand, and the anglers move between pools on foot. No separate car-park coordinate was found.
bottom: Sand: sandbanks, a "shallow, sandy inlet" and "skinny water" between pools that are "sometimes quite deep". Anglers fish from the "sandbank edge" and the "far bank" (Berg River Slam; Earworms and Carp Colours).
permit: CapeNature freshwater angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance), required for "freshwater anglers over the age of six years old ... for fishing in public waters". It costs R45, is valid 12 months and takes 2-5 working days: email an application form and pay by EFT (CapeNature permit page). Indigenous fish such as witvis and Clanwilliam yellowfish must be released. This rule comes from the finders' notes citing CapeNature's recreational-fishing page and was not in the cached text. A permit is needed to move live fish between waters.
legality: Fishing is allowed. The Berg River is a public river: westerncape.gov.za lists it under "The different locations where the public can go fishing", noting "Above Paarl, you'll find smallmouth bass and carp." No MPA, CapeNature reserve or City of Cape Town reserve covers this reach. Checked: the Western Cape Government fishing page and the CapeNature dams-and-rivers permit page (both cached 29 Oct 2026). Neither page gives closed seasons or bag limits for this water. The legal status of the banks at the Arboretum (municipal park or private land) was not confirmed by any source.
description: The Berg River where it flows through Paarl. This lowland reach has pools, sandbanks and shallow sandy inlets, and floods reshape it every winter ("After every winter's high flows, it rearranges itself — new pools, new sandbanks, fresh lies"). Local fly anglers sight-fish it from the bank for "hyper-spooky" carp on small flies such as the Lalu Bug. By-catch includes smallmouth bass ("About 18 inches, fat and red-eyed") and the odd wild rainbow trout, and children catch "small banded Tilapia on a stick rod and float".
hazards: Pollution: Trakoshis (Mar 2020) found an inlet at the top of the Arboretum releasing 'filthy, dirty smelly water'. His dog 'became seriously ill after drinking the water' and he scrubbed his sons after they swam. The inlet was later said to be a stormwater drain and the discharge stopped. Coetzee mentions 'the odd turd and pollution'. Do not drink the water or let dogs drink it; wash hands.
Winter high flows and floods reshape the river every year (new pools and sandbanks), with strong current in places.
Drought: in 2018 the river had 'almost no flow at all and many of the pools turned stagnant'.
The Arboretum section is 'hard to access from the bank' (dense bank vegetation implied).
Wind spoils sight fishing (it 'made sight fishing tough').
access_notes: No source describes parking, a public access point, hours or fees. Local anglers walk the banks from home: Trakoshis walks his dog 'along its banks' daily and watched carp 'feeding from the footbridge'. On the Slam trip the group moved on foot between 'one of our usual haunts', a downstream pool with a sandy inlet, and a second main pool, fishing from the 'far bank' and the 'sandbank edge'. Trakoshis calls the Arboretum section 'hard to access from the bank' and planned to fish it from a paddleboard (not shore fishing). No gate fee is known. Confirm that the bank you use is public, or get the landowner's permission.
unverified: LeRoy Botha starting 'at the foot bridge' with 'a 3-weight and a 7-weight' (from the finders' notes). Not found in 'Earworms and Carp Colours' or 'The Edge of Darkness' when opened on 30 Oct 2026.
The exact stand. The Arboretum is used only as a coordinate anchor; no angling article names it as the place they fish.
Whether the banks at the Arboretum/footbridge are public (municipal) land, and the parking, hours and safety there.

The CapeNature rules that indigenous fish (witvis, Clanwilliam yellowfish) must be released and that most alien species have no bag or size limits. These come from the finders' notes citing capenature.co.za/activities/recreational-fishing; the text was not in the cached evidence.
Spinning with lures for smallmouth bass at Paarl. It is plausible, but only fly catches are reported for this reach.

Witvis presence. The Slam author speculated about 'last summer's stockings' but has seen none; a Mission article calls Berg witvis 'extinct in this river'. A reintroduction at Berg River Resort is reported second-hand (FOSAF, via a search summary).
Best months for any species. Only two dated trips exist (early summer; March, inferred from a photo filename).
Paarl tourism text saying visitors can 'enjoy bass fishing' from the riverbank. Seen only in a search snippet; the paarlonline page now serves unrelated betting content.

issues: Legality holds. westerncape.gov.za/fishing-western-cape (cached 29 Oct 2026) lists the Berg River under 'The different locations where the public can go fishing' and says 'You'll need a license to fish in public rivers and dams.' The CapeNature dams-and-rivers page confirms the R45 licence and 2-5 working days. No MPA applies inland. No cached source shows a reserve, a water-supply dam or a bylaw closure at the Paarl reach. Nominatim (fetched 2 Nov 2026) tags the Arboretum as leisure=park, which fits public municipal land but does not prove there is no bylaw restriction.

The Western Cape Government quote is 'Above Paarl, you'll find smallmouth bass and carp', which literally means upstream of Paarl. The town reach sits on the boundary between that section and the 'further downstream' section, which adds Mozambique tilapia and sharptooth catfish. The record applies the quote to Paarl itself a little loosely.

Small conflict on licence turnaround: the CapeNature page says '2-5 working days', but a cached search summary quotes the same page as 'one working day'. The 2-5 day figure comes from the opened page, so keep it.

Coordinate anchor problem: the only source that names the Arboretum (Trakoshis, 'The Berg River's Pollution Problem') says that section is 'hard to access from the bank' and planned to fish it by stand-up paddleboard. So the anchor sits on the one reach a source calls hard to fish from shore. No angling source places a bank stand at the Arboretum.

The coordinates are the centroid of a park relation whose bounding box is about 2.5 km north-south by 1.25 km east-west (-33.7633 to -33.7404, 18.9672 to 18.9808, Nominatim jsonv2, 2 Nov 2026). The point is inside the named place, so it is not refuted, but it may be several hundred metres from the water's edge. A point on the river bank would be better.

'Earworms and Carp Colours' (fetched 2 Nov 2026) does not mention Paarl, the Arboretum, a footbridge or any named pool; it says only 'the river'. It mentions only common carp: no bass, trout or tilapia. It confirms 'heavily weighted Lalu bugs', Leonard Flemming's 'carp jig fly', 'too much of a plop', a wind problem, 'a clear, sunny day' and an unlanded 'monster'. It gives no month or season, and the byline date (6 April 2022) is the publication date.

species.size: Large river carp. Matt Kennedy's first Berg carp was 26 inches (~66 cm); Trakoshis describes 'a very healthy population of large, streamline river carp' and lost 'a monster'
species.method: fly (sight fishing from the bank); light bait
species.bait: Lalu Bug (weighted for faster current), red squirmy, Flexpole, dragonfly nymph, Leonard Flemming's small carp jig fly
species.notes: The main target. 'Difficult, picky fish' that are 'hyper-spooky' and spooked by casts landing with 'too much of a plop'; 'Plenty of fish about — feeding too — but nothing was eating the flies.' Sight fishing needs clear, sunny days, and wind makes it 'tough'. Carp have been seen 'feeding from the footbridge'. Months are weak evidence: one trip was in early summer ('tadpoles are plentiful in early summer') and one in March 2022, inferred from a photo filename.

species.size: Small
species.bait: Small hooks under a float on a 'stick rod' (bait not named)
species.notes: Trakoshis: his son catches 'small banded Tilapia on a stick rod and float' in the Paarl reach. Mozambique tilapia and sharptooth catfish are listed by the Western Cape Government only for the river 'further downstream' of Paarl, so they are not listed here.

species.size: One reported fish of about 18 inches (~45 cm), 'fat and red-eyed — a proper Berg bruiser'
species.method: fly; spinning with small lures likely but not reported at Paarl
species.bait: Lalu Bug (tiny hooks; the author has lost bass on them)
species.notes: 'There are also some great smallmouth bass in and among the bus carp' (Coetzee). The Western Cape Government and CapeNature list smallmouth bass 'above Paarl'. An invasive alien, blamed for wiping out the Berg witvis.

species.size: One fish reported, size not given ('flawless fins, perfect color')
species.bait: Red squirmy
species.notes: A by-catch while carp fishing in the Paarl reach (Berg River Slam, 1 Nov 2025). Official sources place trout 'above Franschhoek' in the mountain reaches, so expect them only occasionally this far down.

name: Lourens River
area: Somerset West (Helderberg), City of Cape Town
coord_source: Nominatim (OpenStreetMap) result for "Radloff Park, Somerset West", type park, -34.0801549, 18.8727740, fetched 30 Oct 2026. It matches the merge-step point. No angling source names a stand. Radloff Park is used because it is the public riverside park that a Lourens River blog names as its access point (poroderma.substack.com). For reference, Wikipedia gives the Lourens River Protected Natural Environment as 34.078 S, 18.885 E.

access.note: Radloff Park (City park, with a dog park) beside the river in Somerset West. Parking and entry points are not described by any source. Assumed to be the same spot as the stand.

bottom: No source describes it. It is a small mountain-fed urban stream that a snorkeller explored on foot from Radloff Park, which suggests shallow, wadeable water. The substrate is unknown.
mouth: Not applicable to this freshwater reach. The river reaches False Bay at Strand through 'a small estuary' (Wikipedia, Lourens River), next to the Dick Dent Bird Sanctuary. Whether the mouth is open or managed was not sourced.
permit: CapeNature freshwater recreational angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance), valid 12 months. Get it from CapeNature head office 087 087 9262 or the Stellenbosch office 021 866 1560. Upstream estate water (Vergelegen, Lourensford) needs the landowner's permission.
legality: Fishing is allowed with a licence. This is a public river named on the Western Cape Government's fishing page ('You'll need a license to fish in public rivers and dams', issued by CapeNature, valid 12 months). Private reaches upstream (Vergelegen, Lourensford) need the owner's permission (same page: private water needs the owner's permission). The Lourens River Protected Natural Environment was declared 5 Sep 1997. Its Wikipedia page says nothing about angling restrictions, and I could not confirm whether it limits fishing. None of the TMNP, Helderberg or Robben Island MPA rules apply to this freshwater reach. Note for the estuary and mouth at Strand: the beach WEST of the Lourens mouth is the no-take Helderberg MPA. EAST of the mouth to the Gordon's Bay breakwater is a Reg 10(f)(v) closed area where only shore angling is allowed (marine brochures). Treat both as separate from this freshwater record. I did not check City of Cape Town park rules for fishing in Radloff Park.
description: A small urban river (about 23 km long) that runs from the Hottentots Holland mountains through Somerset West to a small estuary at Strand. The Western Cape Government lists it as a public fishing location: rainbow trout are common above Somerset West and carp are common in the middle and lower sections. A 2025 fishing report sums it up as "Catch trout upstream and carp downstream". Radloff Park is the public point of reference. The trout water upstream runs through private estates.
hazards: Water quality: the District Mail (May 2022, 'Our river our responsibility') covers pollution in the river, and a search snippet reports complaints about sewage smell. Wikipedia says the coast near the mouth is in poorer condition because of river pollution.
Private land upstream (Vergelegen, Lourensford): you would be trespassing without permission.
Urban riverside park: personal safety and car security not assessed by any source.
access_notes: Radloff Park in Somerset West is a public City park on the river, with a dog park. No source describes parking, opening hours, fees or paths along the river. The trout reaches upstream are on private wine and farm estates, and no source gives a way in. Indigenous Cape kurper (Sandelia capensis) live in this reach (Poroderma blog). They are not an angling target, so release any caught by accident.
unverified: Any specific public angling stand in the town reach. Radloff Park is a reference point, not a named fishing spot.
Baits, lures, flies, typical sizes and best months for carp and trout on this river.
CapeNature licence fee (the merge step said R45; not confirmed from a fetched page).
Trout closed season on Western Cape streams (not sourced here).
Whether the Lourens River Protected Natural Environment or City of Cape Town park by-laws restrict fishing at Radloff Park.
Somerset West family fly-fishing the upper Lourens (search snippet attributed to bolanderlifestyle.co.za; the fetched page ?p=9582 did not contain it).
Sewage-odour complaints (search snippet only).
Bottom type and depth of the town reach.
Parking, hours and safety at Radloff Park.
Contents of the Tracks4Africa 'Lourens River Flyfishing' listing and the flytalk.co.za 'Lourens River?? Any luck?' thread (both blocked; only their titles are known).

issues: Legality holds up. The City of Cape Town 'Freshwater fishing' page (fetched 2 Nov 2026) says only that anglers over six need a licence for public waters, rivers and state dams, and that fishing needs permission on private land. It does not name the Lourens River, Somerset West or Radloff Park, and it has no City no-fishing rule for rivers or parks. The CapeNature permit page (cached 29 Oct) names the Lourens among its rivers and cites s53 of the Nature Conservation Ordinance. The point is about 4 km inland of the coast, so none of the MPA zones apply. I found no source that shows a prohibition, but no source rules out a restriction from the Lourens River Protected Natural Environment or a park by-law either. That gap is still real.

The Jacita report (6 June 2025) is not independent evidence. Its freshwater section lists the same waters in the same order as the Western Cape Government and CapeNature pages (Brandvlei, Rietvlei, Lakenvlei, Misverstand, Sandvlei, Theewaterskloof, then the Berg, Breede, Eerste/Lourens and Liesbeek rivers), so it is a rewrite of the government list. It should not count as a second, corroborating 'fishing report'. The cached record also gives only a paraphrase ('Trout upstream, carp downstream'), so the exact quote 'Catch trout upstream and carp downstream' cannot be checked against the evidence file.

Evidence is river-level only. The only angling-specific pages are official licence and listing pages (westerncape.gov.za/fishing-western-cape and the CapeNature permit page). They name the Lourens as a public fishing water with carp in the middle and lower sections and trout above Somerset West, and both species suit light tackle. No angling source names Radloff Park or any stand in the town reach, or describes fishing there. The two angling-specific pages that might (the Tracks4Africa 'Lourens River Flyfishing' listing and the flytalk thread) were blocked. This is enough not to refute the spot, but not enough for anything above low confidence.
The CapeNature page itself says 'Carp is common in the middle and lower part of the river' (cached 29 Oct). That is a stronger source than Jacita and should be added to the carp species sources.

The trout claim for the public reach is weaker than the record says. The Poroderma blog is a snorkelling account. The cached extract mentions 'a trout (an invasive species)' and also a crab eating from a dead trout, so the one trout seen may have been dead. The blog says the author first came on the river while taking the dog to Radloff Dog Park. It does not say the trout was seen there. 'Occasional' at the town stand is not supported; 'rare' or 'unconfirmed' fits better. Both government pages put trout above Somerset West, which is mostly private water.

The record lists 'CapeNature licence fee R45' as unverified. The cached CapeNature permit page (29 Oct 2026) says 'The licence costs R45', so that item is confirmed and can come off the unverified list. The 12-month validity comes only from the Western Cape Government page; the CapeNature page does not state a validity period.

species.bait: No source names baits or flies for this river. Small-hook bait rigs for carp are the usual approach, but nothing here confirms that.
species.notes: Western Cape Government: 'Carp are common in the middle and lower sections' of the Eerste and Lourens rivers. Jacita fishing report (6 June 2025): 'Catch trout upstream and carp downstream.' Neither says which reach in town, or gives sizes or a season.

species.bait: No fly patterns sourced for this river.
species.notes: Western Cape Government: 'Rainbow trout are common above ... Somerset West (Lourens).' That upper water is privately owned (Wikipedia: upper reaches 'relatively undisturbed and are privately owned'; Vergelegen and Lourensford estates), so you need the landowner's permission there. At the public town reach the only sign of trout is a snorkeller's blog that came on the river at Radloff Dog Park and saw 'a trout (an invasive species)'. A search snippet also mentions a Somerset West family fly fishing 'the upper regions of the Lourens River', but the page fetched did not contain it. Abundance is set to occasional because that is what the public stand probably offers. Upstream it is common.

name: Eerste River (lower)
aka: Eerste River, middle and lower reaches
area: Stellenbosch town (Die Laan) downstream toward Macassar
coord_source: The merge step's reference point: OSM "Die Laan", a public road along the Eerste River in Stellenbosch town, near where the province says the trout water gives way to carp water. No source names a stand. Not re-geocoded in this pass.
mouth: Not part of this freshwater spot. Wikipedia says the Eerste estuary at Macassar was naturally "a small temporarily open system with little tidal flow" and forms the western boundary of the Helderberg MPA. No source describes how the mouth is managed now.
permit: CapeNature freshwater angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance 19 of 1974, s53), required for anyone over six. It costs R45: email the application form with proof of payment to permits.fax@capenature.co.za and allow 2 to 5 working days. The Western Cape Government says licences are valid for 12 months from issue. CapeNature asks anglers to get permission before fishing on private land, to return indigenous fish, and to hold a permit to transport live fish.
legality: Fishing is allowed with a licence on public stretches. Under section 53 of the Nature Conservation Ordinance 19 of 1974, "no person may fish in any inland waters without an angling licence" (CapeNature permit page). The Western Cape Government also says "You'll need a license to fish in public rivers and dams." The river is fresh water and not in any MPA. The Helderberg MPA runs seaward of the high-water mark from the Eerste mouth east to the Lourens mouth, so the river channel upstream is outside it. No source lists the Eerste as a Cape Piscatorial Society beat, and none makes it a City or provincial reserve below Stellenbosch (Jonkershoek Nature Reserve is the upper river). Not checked: the City of Cape Town freshwater-fishing page, which was blocked, and whether Stellenbosch Municipality allows fishing from its riverside land.
description: The Eerste River from Stellenbosch down toward the Cape Flats. The Western Cape Government's fishing guide lists "rainbow trout above Stellenbosch, with carp in the middle and lower sections." A Durbanville tackle shop's June 2025 report puts it as "Catch trout upstream and carp downstream." No source names a particular bank, so the marker is a public riverside road (Die Laan) in Stellenbosch.
hazards: Much of the bank below Stellenbosch runs through private farmland: get landowner permission (CapeNature advice)
Lowest reach near Macassar: a Macassar Beach source warns the area is dangerous to visit because of increasing crime
River rises sharply after heavy winter rain (Wikipedia shows it in flood in Stellenbosch)
access_notes: No source gives a public access point. The marker is Die Laan, a public road beside the river in Stellenbosch town, with street parking. Whether fishing is allowed from the town's riverside land is unconfirmed. Downstream, the river runs through farms (landowner permission needed) and then through the Cape Flats suburbs to Macassar. Bring a CapeNature licence. There are no gate fees or hours on the town stretch. The Jonkershoek reserve upstream charges R80 per adult and is trout water, not this spot.
unverified: Any named stand or public access point on the middle or lower Eerste; Die Laan is a reference point only
Whether fishing is allowed from Stellenbosch Municipality riverside land at Die Laan, or from City of Cape Town land on the lower reaches (City freshwater-fishing page blocked)
Carp size, best months, and the baits or flies used on this river
Depth, bottom and water quality of the middle and lower reaches
No bag or size limits on carp as an alien species (the CapeNature permit page does not address it)
Drive times are OSRM estimates, not from any source

issues: Legality holds as far as the evidence goes. This is fresh water well inland of the Helderberg MPA, whose northern boundary is the high-water mark (Wikipedia Helderberg MPA page, cached). Cached CapeNature text quotes Ordinance s53 ('no person may fish in any inland waters without an angling licence'), and the WC Government fishing page says 'You'll need a license to fish in public rivers and dams', valid 12 months. Nothing in the cache shows a ban. Still unchecked: Stellenbosch Municipality rules for its riverside land at Die Laan, and City of Cape Town rules on the lower reaches (the City freshwater-fishing page was blocked).

The two 'independent' angling sources are probably one. The Jacita 6 June 2025 report (in the cache under scratchpad/fw3 and fp3, not in this spot's evidence file) runs Berg, Breede, 'Eerste and Lourens', Liesbeek in the same order with the same content as the westerncape.gov.za/fishing-western-cape river list. It looks like a paraphrase of the provincial page, so carp on this stretch rests on one government species list, not two confirmations.

No source describes anyone fishing the middle or lower Eerste: no bank, stand, method, bait, season or catch. A search aimed at it ('Kuils River OR Eerste River lower reaches carp catfish ... sealine fishingowl') found nothing angling-specific beyond the provincial list. The only Eerste angling write-up in the cache (The Mission, themissionflymag.com/?p=66753, LeRoy Botha 2020) is about trout and dry fly near Stellenbosch, which is upstream water and not this spot. The evidence is thin but not refuted: the provincial fishing guide does name carp in the middle and lower sections, and bank carp fishing fits light bait tackle.

Carp abundance 'common' is not supported by a fetched page. Both cached fetches of westerncape.gov.za/fishing-western-cape say only 'carp in the middle and lower parts/sections'. The word 'common' appears only in search-engine summaries, and one of those (evidence line 125) attaches 'common' to the trout above Stellenbosch, so it may have been carried over to carp by mistake. Set abundance to unknown or present.

The description and species notes put the provincial wording in quotation marks ('rainbow trout above Stellenbosch, with carp in the middle and lower sections'). That text is the fetch tool's paraphrase, not confirmed verbatim page text.

Marker placement: the coordinates match OSM Die Laan (Nominatim cached result -33.9386823, 18.8667170, 'Die Laan, a residential road in Stellenbosch Central'), so they are not wrong for the named point. But Die Laan is in Stellenbosch town, which the province gives as the trout/carp boundary ('trout above Stellenbosch'). The marker therefore sits at the edge of the documented carp water, not in the 'middle and lower' sections downstream. No source names a better point, so no new coordinates are proposed.

species.method: light bait or fly (not stated by any source for this river)
species.notes: Western Cape Government: 'Eerste River: rainbow trout above Stellenbosch, with carp in the middle and lower sections' (search summary: carp 'common' there). Jacita tackle-shop report, 6 June 2025: 'Eerste and Lourens Rivers: Catch trout upstream and carp downstream.' Neither gives size, season, bait or a named stretch. Rainbow trout are upstream of Stellenbosch (Jonkershoek), not on this stretch.

name: Smalblaar River
area: Du Toitskloof, along the N1 east of the Huguenot Tunnel (Rawsonville side)
coord_source: Rough coordinate from the merge step: an OpenStreetMap point on the river beside the N1, just east of the Huguenot Tunnel exit. It is near the Beat 6 and Transport parking at the weighbridge, which the CPS page puts about 250 m from the tunnel exit. It is not a surveyed stand. The CPS page places the other beats by road distance from the tunnel exit: Hotel and Beats 4-5 at 4 km (Du Kloof Lodge), Beat 3 at the weir at 5.5 km, and Beat 1 Picnic at 6.7 km, just past the Klip River bridge. A Nominatim query (30 Oct 2026) returns 'Smalblaarrivier' only for the lower river toward Rawsonville (bbox -33.716 to -33.656, 19.282 to 19.351), so OSM names the reach near the tunnel differently from the CPS.
bottom: Freestone with boulders: the stream 'flows crystal clear through an assortment of boulder sizes' (The Mission, 2024). There are runs and pools, a few too deep to wade on Donkergat (Beat 3), and an artificial weir at the end of Beat 2.
permit: Cape Piscatorial Society water: members only, with river rights and a booked beat; the club's river season is 1 September to 31 May. CapeNature licence and the Limietberg reserve fee too. You need a CapeNature freshwater angling licence (Nature Conservation Ordinance; R45, 12 months) plus a CPS beat booking and day or season river permit. CPS membership is optional for day permits but recommended (R122 start-up, R680 a year, R370 river rights). Local CPS rules: barbless hooks, catch and release with no take at all, and a different member must book Beat 4 and Beat 5 when they are fished together. Fly-only is not stated on the Smalblaar page but is likely (see unverified).
legality: Fishing is allowed with permits. The CPS Smalblaar page (piscator.co.za, fetched 30 Oct 2026) says fishing must be booked in advance with the CPS, sells day permits to members and non-members, makes barbless hooks mandatory, and enforces catch and release: 'The CPS enforces a strict no take limit, and even injured fish must be returned to the ecosystem.' The Mission ('Fishing permits and licenses', 18 Aug 2025) says the CPS 'provides regulated public access' to the Smalblaar/Molenaars, that 'A booking is always required', and that anglers also need 'a registered Cape Nature freshwater angling permit'. The CPS report of 8 Oct 2026 on FOSAF says the Smalblaar/Molenaars system 'has been busy' with fair-to-good catches, closed only 16-18 Oct for SAFFA trials. CapeNature closed the neighbouring Elandspad after the May 2026 floods, but that closure does not apply to the Smalblaar. This is inland fresh water, so no MPA applies, and it is not a City of Cape Town reserve. The winter closed season runs to 1 September (CPS report of 7 Aug 2026).
description: A clear, boulder-strewn freestone trout stream beside the N1 east of the Huguenot Tunnel in Du Toitskloof. The Cape Piscatorial Society splits it into eight bookable beats of 0.5 to 1.2 km, from Ravens Crag near the tunnel down to the Picnic Beat 6.7 km east. Anglers fish it with very light fly gear (an 'Echo River Glass 2-weight', '7x' tippet, Para-Adams, RAB and #20 midge dry flies) for mainly rainbow trout, all released on barbless hooks.
hazards: The N1 runs right beside the river: you park on the island between the carriageways for Beat 1 and walk footpaths off the national road for Beats 4 and 5
Beat 6 Ravens Crag ends at an impassable waterfall in a narrow gorge with steep cliffs and is often fished only up to the Krom River confluence
Some pools on Donkergat (Beat 3) are too deep to wade
Slippery boulder wading in clear, cold water; good wading boots are needed
Dense Rooi Els trees overhang Beat 6 and make casting hard
Floods: the May 2026 floods washed away the neighbouring Elandspad trail and changed rivers in the area
Wrong parking can be fined (CPS)
access_notes: Each beat has its own parking (CPS Smalblaar page). Beat 6 and Transport: park near the weighbridge about 250 m from the tunnel exit, reached by the side road under the N1 bridge. Beat 4, Beat 5 and Hotel: turn into Du Kloof Lodge 4 km from the tunnel exit and use the CPS members' parking through the wooden-pole entrance, then a footpath off the N1. Beat 3: park at the weir, 5.5 km from the tunnel exit. Beat 1 Picnic: park on the island between the N1 carriageways, 6.7 km east of the tunnel exit, just past the Klip River bridge. None of these parking spots has its own coordinates. This is Cape Piscatorial Society water. Every visit must be booked with the CPS in advance, through the CPS app or office. Day permits are sold to members and non-members, and members can buy season permits. Each angler also needs a CapeNature freshwater angling licence (R45, valid 12 months). CPS costs quoted by The Mission: R122 start-up, R680 a year, plus R370 for river rights. Barbless hooks are compulsory and every fish goes back, injured fish included. The CPS page warns that parking in the wrong place can earn a fine. Rivers close over winter: the CPS report of 7 Aug 2026 said all rivers were closed until 1 September. The river was also closed 16-18 Oct 2026 for SAFFA trials. Bring good wading boots and warm clothing for early mornings and late afternoons, especially on Beat 6. The route is the N1 through the Huguenot Tunnel, which is a toll road.
unverified: Fly-only rule on the Smalblaar: the CPS Smalblaar page does not state it. A search summary says the Elandspad is fly-only, and The Mission calls CPS waters 'fly fishing venues', so spinning is probably not allowed. Confirm with the CPS before using lures.
Brown trout in the Smalblaar: the merge notes list them, but no Smalblaar-specific page names them. The CPS page says 'mainly rainbow trout'.
Exact closed-season dates: only the CPS report of 7 Aug 2026 ('all rivers are now closed until September 1') was found. The start date, about 1 June, comes from merge notes and is not confirmed.
Whether a CapeNature Limietberg conservation or entry fee applies on the N1 beats, as it does for the Elandspad trail. Not stated on the CPS page.
Exact coordinates of each beat's parking. Only road distances from the tunnel exit are published.
Whether the CPS rule to kill all bass ('as is the case for the rivers', FOSAF report) matters here: no bass are reported in the Smalblaar.

issues: Legality holds. I re-fetched the CPS Smalblaar page on 3 Nov 2026 (piscator.co.za/CPS2/streams/smalblaar/). It says fishing 'must be booked in advance with the CPS', that day permits are sold to members and non-members, that barbless hooks are mandatory, and that catch and release is enforced ('strict no take limit, and even injured fish must be returned'). It also says access is controlled jointly by the CPS and Cape Nature Conservation, which manages the Limietberg reserve. The record leaves out that joint control and should add it. The FOSAF report of 8 Oct 2026 (CPS secretary) says the river is open and busy, apart from the SAFFA closure on 16-18 Oct. No MPA or City of Cape Town rule applies to inland water here.

Legality caveat the record leaves out: The Mission's 'Cape Streams Loading' (18 Sep 2025, in the evidence) reports that CapeNature told the CPS, 'mere days before the Cape trout stream season opened', of a decision about the four Limietberg rivers. It warns of 'No beat system' and 'an unregulated free-for-all'. The 2026 CPS page and the 2026 FOSAF report show the CPS booking system still running, so this is not a refutation. Still, the governance is contested and the access_notes should say so.

The CPS Smalblaar page the record cites as 'fetched 30 Oct 2026' is not in the 29 Oct evidence cache. My re-fetch confirms its main claims: the beats, the parking distances, the rules and 3 lb trophy fish. The exact phrases quoted as 'mainly rainbow trout' and 'fair-sized and well-bred' were not confirmed word for word. The fetch gave 'a good head of fair-sized rainbow trout' that breed well and have not been stocked for many years.

Beat count is wrong. The CPS page lists the Transport Beat as 'Coming soon...', so there are seven bookable beats plus one not yet open, not 'eight bookable beats' as the description and verdict reason say.

Size claim misplaced. The CPS page puts the 15-inch fish in the Krom River tributary ('Fish of 15 inches have been seen feasting in the tiny, shallow pools along this stream'), not in the Smalblaar around the Krom confluence on Beat 6.

Months [9,10,11,12] are an inference, and the CPS page contradicts it. The page says the Smalblaar's upper kloof water stays cool and 'the fish do particularly well here in the warmer months', compared with lower beats such as the Molenaars. Davis's tough February 2014 trip on Smalblaar 3 was about the lower beats. Summer months should not be left out on that basis alone.

species.size: The CPS calls them 'fair-sized and well-bred', with trophy fish of about 3 lb (1.4 kg) still caught each year. Rainbows of about 15 inches are noted around the Krom River confluence on Beat 6. No typical weight is published.
species.bait: Small dry flies: Para-Adams and para-RAB on the Picnic Beat (2024), a 'dancing RAB' and a '#20 midge' on 7x tippet on Smalblaar 3 (Feb 2014). Fish were rising to small black mayflies. Rods around 2-weight.
species.notes: The CPS page says 'mainly rainbow trout'. Catches were fair to good in early Oct 2026. The water is clear and the fish are wary: 'the fish don't give you a second cast' (Fred Davis, 2014), and they were 'Almost impossible to catch at this point. Almost…' (Kennedy, 2024). 'February and March is a always a tough time of the year for the lower beats' with 'thin water, wisened trout' (Davis). A CPS writer says that in late summer and early autumn 'I seldom fish the Smalblaar and focus my time on the Elandspad' (FOSAF, CPS Softy). The best months are therefore the spring opening, September to December. All fish are released.

name: Molenaars River
area: Du Toitskloof valley beside the N1, east of the Huguenot Tunnel towards Rawsonville (Breede tributary)
coord_source: Cape Piscatorial Society Molenaars page (fetched 30 Oct 2026). The stand is the large graffiti rock beside the footpath from the parking, at S33 42.723 E19 11.784, which the page calls the downstream end of the lower beat. The page puts the other end at the rapids above the swing-bridge pool, S33 42.112 E19 12.159 (-33.7019, 19.2027). Its upstream/downstream wording looks reversed against these coordinates, since the river flows north-east towards Rawsonville. The merge step's earlier point, the OSM Molenaarsrivier node at Goudini (-33.6969, 19.2161), lies further downstream and was replaced.

access.note: CPS parking for the lower beat, at S33 42.822 E19 11.791: a side road on the left of the N1 heading east, 8.5 km past the Huguenot Tunnel exit (about 4.5 km past Du Kloof Lodge), where the road starts to rise again. For the upper beat, park at a gate about 5 km past Du Toit's Kloof Lodge towards Worcester and take the path down to the river.

bottom: Freestone mountain stream: rapids, larger pools, wider runs and shallow boulder pocket water. The CPS page gives "pools, runs, pocket water". A kayaking page grades the river class 2 to 4.
permit:
Cape Piscatorial Society water: members only, with river rights and a booked beat; the club's river season is 1 September to 31 May. CapeNature licence too. 1. A CapeNature freshwater angling licence (R45 admin fee; apply by email to permits.fax@capenature.co.za with EFT proof).
2. A CPS beat booking, made at least a day in advance through the CPS office or the CPS app. The Mission (2025) says "a booking is always needed", while membership is "in most cases" not required.
3. CPS fees as published in 2023: R122 start-up, R680 annual membership and R370 for river rights.
Local rules: barbless hooks, strict no-take catch and release, and kill any bass caught (the CPS river rule as reported by FOSAF). The rivers close in winter, roughly June to August, and reopened on 1 September in 2026. The system was closed for SAFFA trials on 16 to 18 October 2026.
legality: Fishing is allowed under Cape Piscatorial Society rules. This is a freshwater river nowhere near an MPA. The CPS lists Molenaars among its club streams (piscator.co.za). The Mission Fly Magazine (18 Aug 2025) says the CPS provides "regulated public access" to the "Smalblaar/Molenaars" under agreements with CapeNature, the Hexvallei Waterboard, MCSA and private landowners. CapeNature names the Molenaars among the Breede tributaries on its freshwater licence page, and Section 53 of the Nature Conservation Ordinance requires a licence for any inland water. Checked on the CPS Molenaars page: catch and release only, barbless hooks mandatory, booking at least a day ahead.
description: The Molenaars is the lower end of the Smalblaar in the Du Toitskloof valley beside the N1. It is a Cape Piscatorial Society trout stream with "larger pools, wider runs and shallow pocket water". The CPS calls it "an early summer beat" because the shallow water heats up quickly. It is fished with dry flies under barbless, catch-and-release rules, and beats are booked through the CPS at least a day in advance.
hazards: Steep, slippery descent from the N1 to the river, plus a farm-fence crossing; the CPS says don't fish the lower beat alone
Walking along the N1 verge from the parking to the cable bridge (highway traffic)
The river rises very fast after rain and drops quickly (kayaking guide); it has class 2 to 4 rapids
Shallow water warms quickly in summer: fish are scarce and stressed outside the early season, and water is extracted for vineyards below the beat
Remote mountain kloof with no facilities
access_notes: Drive the N1 east through the Huguenot Tunnel and park on the side road 8.5 km past the tunnel exit (S33 42.822 E19 11.791). Walk down the N1 to a cable bridge over the river, then down a steep, slippery mountainside and through a farm fence to the water. The CPS says the lower beat "requires good fitness, and stable feet" and asks anglers not to fish it alone. The lower beat is 1.3 km long. The upper beat runs upstream from a spray-painted rock to the start of Smalblaar beat 1, reached by parking at a gate about 5 km past Du Toit's Kloof Lodge. No gate fee or hours are stated for this beat. It is on CPS-leased and farm land, not inside the Limietberg reserve's gated area.
unverified: Whether the CPS rules make the Molenaars fly-only. The beat page says "strict guidelines" and barbless catch and release but does not explicitly ban spinning; the Mission calls CPS waters "fly fishing venues". Treat it as fly water.

issues: Legality holds. This is an inland trout stream in the Du Toitskloof valley, nowhere near any MPA. The CPS Molenaars page (fetched 3 Nov 2026) says the beat 'is on private land' and that access is 'strictly controlled by the Cape Piscatorial Society', booked at least a day ahead. It is a private water, but the public can get in through the CPS (Mission Fly Mag ?p=81250 says 'regulated public access', 'a booking is always needed'). The CapeNature licence page names the Molenaars as a Breede tributary and cites s53 of the Ordinance. The permit statement is not materially wrong. The record should add the CPS page's own 'private land' wording, so nobody reads the beat as open public water.

Coord_source misreads the CPS page. The page gives the lower beat as 'Starts' at S33 42.112 E19 12.159 (the rapids above the swing-bridge pool) and ending at S33 42.723 E19 11.784, the graffiti/spray-painted rock that is also the lower beat's upper boundary and the start of the upper beat. The graffiti rock is therefore the UPSTREAM end, not 'the downstream end of the lower beat'. Anglers walk down the N1 to the cable bridge and fish upstream back towards the parking. That fits the north-east flow towards Goudini/Rawsonville (Nominatim Molenaarsrivier points run from -33.7277,19.1008 near the tunnel to -33.6969,19.2161 at Goudini). Nothing is reversed. The pin itself is fine: it sits on the beat, about 180 m from the CPS parking GPS, and the start-to-end straight line (~1.27 km) matches the page's 1.3 km.

Permit field: the SAFFA closure of 16 to 18 October 2026 has already passed (today is 3 Nov 2026). FOSAF (8 Oct 2026) also puts it under the Smalblaar heading ('the river will be closed'), so the record's 'the system was closed' overstates it. Drop it or mark it as a past one-off.
Species size: the CPS page says 'the biggest fish – up to 20 inches' are taken in the lower section. My fetch did not support the word 'routinely', so treat it as an upper bound, not a typical catch.

Months 9 to 12: the CPS page backs Sep to Nov ('early summer beat', 'seldom fished outside of the early season'). December is when the page says the shallow water 'heats up quickly' and fish become scarce, so December is marginal, not regular.

The rainbow trout species is now verified. westerncape.gov.za/fishing-western-cape (re-read 3 Nov 2026) says 'rainbow trout dominate its mountain streams flowing into it (e.g. Elandsplaat, Holsloot and Molenaars rivers)'. The matching 'unverified' item can come off the list. The CPS Molenaars page itself mentions neither brown trout nor bass.

species.size: The CPS gives no typical size. It says the biggest fish, "up to 20 inches" (about 50 cm), are "routinely taken" in the lower section.
species.bait: Early season: "larger terrestrial insect imitations work well". Summer, when the water thins: "smaller CDC and parachute patterns fished of fine tippets become essential" (CPS). Barbless hooks only.
species.notes: The CPS page says only "trout". The Western Cape Government fishing page says rainbow trout "dominate the mountain streams" feeding the Breede, "such as the Elandsplaat, Holsloot, and Molenaars rivers". All fish must go back: the CPS "enforces a strict no take limit, and even injured fish must be returned". The CPS calls the lower beat "an early summer beat" that is "seldom fished outside of the early season". In summer, fish can be "few and far between". Rivers were closed until 1 September in 2026 (FOSAF, 7 Aug 2026). FOSAF's 8 Oct 2026 report says that with the Elandspad closed, "the Smalblaar/Molenaars system has been busy, and catches are fair to good".
